text: Timing sales around harvest matters because supply changes through the year — when many farmers harvest the same commodity at the same time, competition among sellers can put downward pressure on farm-gate price, though this is a general seasonal pattern, not a guarantee for any specific year in Preah Vihear. A farmer able to safely store a non-perishable product may have the option to delay some sales, but the correct comparison is future selling price minus drying, storage, transport, pest control, spoilage, weight loss, financing cost, and the risk that the future price falls — not simply "harvest price vs. future price." This is especially important for smallholders who may need immediate cash for loan repayment, inputs, household expenses, or the next crop. Rice production in Preah Vihear (e.g., Rovieng district) is heavily rain-dependent, so the production calendar and harvest timing vary by variety and rainfall rather than following one universal month. Cassava is much less flexible than dried grain because fresh roots deteriorate quickly — "harvest now, store for months, sell later" generally does not apply. Cashew can offer more flexibility once properly dried and stored, but only if drying/storage/pest-control costs are less than the expected price gain. During the wet season (roughly May–October), difficulty drying and muddy roads argue for selling sooner rather than risking quality loss while waiting; during the dry season (roughly November–April), drying is often easier but storage still needs protection from heat, dust, and pests. A practical partial-sale strategy — selling enough to cover immediate needs and storing only what can be safely managed — is often more realistic than an all-or-nothing decision.
